chapter_theme: In the last ilampakam the sage Madhavan tells the king what gifts to the restrained and to the unrestrained yield in later births, describes the land of enjoyment and its lovers, and then sets out release as the burning of karma by knowledge, faith and conduct, so that the king bathes in the sermon.

cast.role: the hero, now an old king, who hears the sage
the sage (named 'great ascetic') who preaches the fruit of gifts and the way to release
the pious householder who receives the ascetic
the ascetic who comes to the householder's house
the twin boy and girl born in the land of enjoyment to those who gave rightly
the elder parents of the twins, who die and are born as gods
the girl of the land of enjoyment
the youth of the land of enjoyment

2824.reading: The sage describes the ascetics who wither the five senses, steady the mind that sees the true nature of things, and guard themselves from lying, killing, theft and lust, shining like the cool moon.
2824.nuance: The verse and the next four read as the sage's own continuing talk on gifts to ascetics, though no speaker is named; the narrator may be speaking.

claims.claim: an ascetic must wither the five senses and keep from lying, killing, theft and lust

2825.reading: Whether men torment these ascetics with the adze at every hair-root or bow at their feet with sandal paste, the ascetics weigh both, take them as old deeds, and call no one kin or stranger.
2825.nuance: வாய்ச்சி is taken here as the adze; the cruelty named is slow and deliberate, so the ideal is not a forbearing of a moment's insult but of torture.

claims.claim: ill-treatment and honour alike are the fruit of old deeds and must be met with equal mind

2826.reading: With eyes fixed a yoke's length ahead as the scripture teaches, like a rutting elephant under the moon, the ascetic comes to the house of the worthy householder, who bows to him like a bent bough.
2826.nuance: Who is called விழுத்தவர் (the worthy) and whether the bower is the householder or the ascetic is not fixed by the grammar; the reading follows the next verse, where the householder washes the feet.
2826.event: An ascetic walking by the rule of the scripture reaches a householder's house and is greeted with a bow.

claims.claim: a householder must greet a visiting ascetic with joined hands and a bow

2827.reading: The householder joins his hands, seats the ascetic on a clean floor, removes his dusty cloth, washes and praises his feet, worships with sandal, aloe smoke and flowers, and gives the four nectars to the one restrained in the three.
2827.nuance: The four nectars are not named in the verse. Reading 'in the three' as mind, speech and body is the usual Jain reading of the three restraints, supplied here from outside the Tamil.
2827.event: The householder receives the ascetic, washes his feet, worships him and gives him food.

claims.claim: a gift is rightly given to one restrained in the three (mind, speech and body) after worship of his feet

2828.reading: The sage ranks gifts: given in the nine-fold way to the best it is highest, giving in kindness is middle, and for those who kill animals to feed others, though they give good wealth, the fruit cannot be reckoned by us.
2828.nuance: The syntax of lines 3-4 is hard; whether the fruit is 'unknowable' or simply 'not counted' is not fixed. The 'middle' gift (இடை) is the one 2841 later rewards.

claims.claim: a gift paid for by killing animals yields no fruit that can be reckoned

2829.reading: The sage turns to the king, whose sharp spear is like Death's tongue, tells him to listen well, and promises to tell the fruit of gifts made to those of peerless merit.
2829.event: The sage begins to tell the king what gifts to the worthy yield.

2830.reading: A hand with ringed fingers drives the bellows and the hair of the bellows roars, so that the fire, like a bursting golden lotus, heats the iron lying in it as far as the iron will take.
2830.nuance: The sentence continues into 2831, where the heated iron takes water in proportion to its heating; this verse gives only the forge, and its meaning waits on the next.

2831.reading: As heated iron drinks water in the measure of its heating, merit is in the measure of the gift; the soul steeped in it leaves the body and, after the fixed days, enters a womb by fate.
2831.nuance: The iron and water give a quantitative law of merit, which the Kural (222) and the Purananuru (134) both refuse to put on a ledger.

claims.claim: the merit of a gift is exactly as great as the gift, and it carries the soul to its next birth

2832.reading: After nine months in the womb the giver is born as one of a pair of twins like a jewelled doll wrapped in fine cloth, and their two elder parents pass away.
2832.nuance: சிங்கினார் is read as 'passed away' (the parents' death at the birth), not as a sneeze; this is the sense the sequel supports.
2832.event: Twins are born in the land of enjoyment, and their parents die.

claims.claim: those who gave rightly are reborn as twins in the land of enjoyment

2833.reading: The dead parents are born as gods, their bodies in the heavens dissolving like cloud in the sky; the sage says he will now describe the children.
2833.event: The parents die and are born as gods.

claims.claim: those who die in the land of enjoyment are reborn as gods

2834.reading: The children grow up with no care from anyone and reach full measure in arts, qualities and limbs within the fifty days less one.
2834.nuance: The unit of fifty less one is not named; days is assumed.
2834.event: The twins grow to perfection with no rearing.

2835.reading: Under a wishing tree that gives garlands, ornaments, bracelets and cloth, a girl whose voice is like the palai lute stands among gem-set boughs, like a grove of stars and moon in flower.
2835.nuance: There is no day or night under the tree; the setting is outside the world of cause and labour.
2835.event: A girl of the land of enjoyment stands under a wishing tree.

2836.reading: A youth, spring's king to the eye, rises with sandal on his shoulders, ear-ornaments shining and a wishing-tree garland hanging on his chest, and comes up to her.
2836.event: The youth of the land of enjoyment approaches the girl.

2837.reading: As he comes by fate, ear-rings shining and his garland swinging, he sees her standing like a doll made of sea nectar, and their hearts are joined in love as one.
2837.event: The youth sees the girl and the two fall in love.

2838.reading: The girl's breasts, like two jewel pitchers brimming with desire's wine, wearing pearls at their tips, burn the eyes of those who look and press against the garland.
2838.nuance: Pure description of the girl; it builds the picture of enjoyment as the first fruit of giving.

2839.reading: The younger girl's eyes, blinking in a quarrel of love, seem to rebuke him for slighting her, and when his hair garland touches her anklets as he bows, he is given the feast of a smile.
2839.nuance: The quarrel and appeasement of the akam tradition is carried into the heaven-like land; the love is not tested by lack or separation.
2839.event: After a lovers' quarrel the youth bows at her feet and is forgiven with a smile.

2840.reading: They go to tall mansions, golden groves, play the jewelled lute, bathe in flower pools and drink old wealth, and are bound by the garland of desire.
2840.nuance: 'Bound' (பிணிக்கப் பட்டார்) holds the verse's turn: the reward is itself a binding, which 2610 shows ruining Saccandan.
2840.event: The pair spend their days in pleasure in the land of enjoyment.

claims.claim: pleasure enjoyed there is the fruit of old merit and also a bond

2841.reading: Whatever the wide-eyed and the golden-hilled youth wish for, the wishing trees give; those who did the middle sort of gift enjoy this and spend it, O king, lord of the two treasures of the world of deeds.
2841.nuance: 'The world of deeds' (கரும பூமி) is where the king lives, set against this land where nothing is done and all is enjoyed.

claims.claim: a gift of the middle sort is rewarded by whatever one desires in the land of enjoyment

2842.reading: Those who gave to the unrestrained are born, by the fruit of that gift, on one of the many islands in the roaring sea, with bodies and faces unlike those of men, eating the fruit of their fate.
2842.nuance: The recipient decides the fruit: the same giving, given to one who has no restraint, is repaid with a debased birth, and the doctrine is told to Civakan, who is called a lion in rage.

claims.claim: a gift to the unrestrained is rewarded by birth with a strange body on a sea-island

2843.reading: Those who wear the jewel-garland of virtue become gods in the heavens; others rule the whole earth under one umbrella and take delight in their wheel of command, O lord.
2843.nuance: The verse ranks the fruit of virtue above the fruit of worldly rule. Who rules under one umbrella (the cakravartin) is a recipient of the second sort, which the king hearing it may recognise as himself.

claims.claim: virtue (sila) brings rebirth as a god in a heaven
another sort of merit brings a world-ruler's umbrella and delights

2844.reading: The sage turns to the nature of release, saying it lies in the scripture of the lord under the three umbrellas, who sits beneath the flowering pindi tree.
2844.nuance: The three umbrellas and the pindi (ashoka) tree are the Jina's regalia in the Jain account; here they name the source of authority for what follows.

claims.claim: release is taught in the scripture of the Jina under the pindi tree

2845.reading: Knowing 'this is the real thing' is knowledge, seeing it clearly is faith, and holding both firmly within oneself, with both kinds of pain dropped, is conduct.
2845.nuance: The Jain triad of knowledge, faith and conduct is set out as a definition; the 'two' in line 3 is not named in the verse.

claims.claim: right knowledge is knowing what is real
right faith is clear seeing of it
right conduct is holding both firmly within, free of the two bonds

2846.reading: These three together are like a blazing fire that burns the tree of deeds standing in rows, and release is to be free of deeds; the fourfold infinite is then won.
2846.nuance: Karma is destroyed by effort, not by a god or by grace; the verse closes with the 'fourfold' (அநந்த நான்மை) that 2847 spells out.

claims.claim: knowledge, faith and conduct together burn away karma, and that is release
release gives the fourfold infinite

2847.reading: These are the four: endless knowledge, endless seeing, endless power and endless joy, with the qualities named; those who have them rise to the upper world.

claims.claim: the liberated soul has endless knowledge, perception, energy and bliss and goes up to the upper world

2848.reading: The sage, named 'great ascetic', is like a mountain whose coral-lipped mouth lets the water of the first dharma fall like a stream, and the king bathes in it to lose the stain of great sorrow.
2848.nuance: The sage is called 'great ascetic' but not by another name in these verses; the metaphor makes hearing a bath.
2848.event: The king, hearing the sage's sermon, is cleansed of sorrow as if bathing in a falling stream.

claims.claim: the sage's teaching of dharma washes away the stain of great sorrow

links.note: 2824 names what the ascetics do to quench the five senses (wither them, keep from four sins); Kural 25 says only that the strength of one who has quenched them is witnessed by Indra.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the strength of one who has quenched the senses without the practice, and the verse gives the practice without the strength, so the two together show both sides.

gains.a: the verse's practice of withering the senses gets a measure of what it wins, a strength that heaven's king himself would witness
gains.b: the Kural's quenching of the five gets a concrete discipline (withering the body, keeping from lying, killing, theft and lust) that its praise leaves open

links.note: 2824 has the ascetic wither the five senses and so subdue them by effort; Tirumanthiram 140 says the senses come under control of themselves once the Lord is met.
links.teaches: One text holds that the senses are conquered by the ascetic's own labour, the other that they are conquered by meeting the Lord, so the two disagree on who does the work.

gains.a: the verse's effortful mortification is shown to be one of two ways to the same end, and the one that leaves out a god
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram verse's claim that no effort is needed meets its rival, a school that does not wait for grace

links.note: 2831 says merit is measured by the gift as iron takes water in proportion to its heating, a gift for the next birth; Purananuru 134 says Ay is no trader who buys virtue with gifts for the next life.
links.teaches: The verse sets a gift's reward in an exact ledger, and the Sangam poem names that ledger as what its patron does not do.

gains.a: the doctrine of measured merit, shown from outside, looks like the trade it is accused of in the Sangam poem
gains.b: the poem's refusal of a 'trader's' giving gains a worked-out doctrine of gift-for-fruit that makes the refusal pointed

links.note: 2841 says the middle sort of gift is paid by whatever one wishes in the land of enjoyment; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world.
links.teaches: The Cintamani ties each gift to its reward, while the Kural cuts giving loose from reward by a hypothetical.

gains.a: the verse's rewards (wishing trees for the middle gift) are shown as one of the things the Kural's hypothetical sets aside
gains.b: the Kural's hypothetical gets a full account of the other-worldly rewards it asks us to imagine away

links.note: 2842 ranks gifts by the receiver, with a debased birth for a gift to the unrestrained; Kural 221 says only giving to those who have nothing is giving.
links.teaches: The Kural names the needy as the only true recipient, but the Cintamani's sage names the restrained, so who deserves a gift is answered in opposite ways.

gains.a: the verse's grading of recipients by restraint is set against the Kural's grading by need
gains.b: the Kural's 'the destitute' is shown as one possible answer, where the sage answers 'the restrained'

links.note: 2845 defines release's path as knowledge, faith and conduct together; Kural 356 says those who learned here and saw the real thing reach the path of not coming back.
links.teaches: The Kural pairs learning and seeing, and the Jain verse adds the third (holding it in conduct), so the two give different recipes for the same release.

gains.a: the verse's triad is shown as a larger version of the Kural's learning and seeing
gains.b: the Kural's two-part path is given a third part that the verse insists cannot be left out

links.note: 2846 says knowledge, faith and conduct together are a fire that burns the tree of deeds; Tirumanthiram 117 says the malas burn only in the sun's presence, as the sunstone burns cotton only in the sun.
links.teaches: Both burn the impurity by fire, but one fire is the seeker's own three virtues and the other needs the Lord's sun.

gains.a: the verse's fire of karma is shown to burn on its own, which the sunstone image says it cannot
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's sunstone gets a rival that claims the stone burns without a sun

links.note: 2847 names what the freed soul has (endless knowledge, seeing, power and joy); Kural 362 says to want, want not to be born.
links.teaches: The Kural describes release as an absence of birth and desire, and the Cintamani's sage describes it as a fullness, so one calls release emptying and the other filling.

gains.a: the verse's release is set beside the Kural's, which describes it only as not being born again
gains.b: the Kural's release by not wanting gets an account of what the one released then has

links.note: In 2622 Vijayai says that all who are born are greedy, never give a handful, and should give their wealth away; in 2829 the sage promises to tell what gifts to the worthy yield.
links.teaches: The mother's plea to give and the sage's account of what giving earns are two halves of one argument, one urging, one promising.

links.note: In 2840 the pair are bound by the garland of desire in the pleasure that their gifts earned; in 2610 Saccandan, swallowed by pleasure, would not come out and fell.
links.teaches: Pleasure that is the fruit of merit is still a bond, and the story of the old king shows what happens when one stays bound.

links.note: In 2619 Vijayai tells the people to do hard penance and give before youth lapses; in 2848 the king bathes in the sage's dharma-water and loses the stain of sorrow.
links.teaches: The mother's exhortation and the sage's sermon reach the same hearer in the same ilampakam, and the sermon is what makes the king act on them.

source_issues: Verses 2824-2827 and 2835-2843 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2826 line 3 and 2828 lines 3-4 are hard to parse; readings are marked uncertain.
2834 line 3 gives a number (fifty less one) with no unit.
